title: Jesus Christ: An Artifice for Aggression
byline: by Sita Ram Goel · Voice of India · 1994
lede: In 1956 a Jesuit friend tried to convert Goel and showed him gospel passages claiming Jesus was the only way to God. Decades later, influenced by Ram Swarup's critique of monotheism, Goel returned to the subject. His complaint is with Hindus: they object to the missions but praise Jesus, and so invent a “real” Jesus and a “true” Christianity. He draws on two centuries of Western scholarship on the historical Jesus, from Reimarus to Schweitzer and Bultmann, to argue that the gospel figure cannot be recovered from history. He says the missions should be met on doctrine, not only on conduct.
facts: the Jesuit's attempt to convert him, in Patna
chapters: history, fiction, faith, decline in the West
Schweitzer's Quest of the Historical Jesus, his central witness
appendices, including letters with an English correspondent
note: This is a deliberately provocative polemic, and much of its language is harsh; this page does not repeat it. Goel leans on the “Christ myth” view that Jesus may not have existed, which most historians, religious and secular, reject. They accept a historical Jesus while agreeing the gospels are not straightforward biography. Schweitzer, whom Goel quotes, was attacking the 19th-century theologians' portraits of Jesus, not denying that Jesus lived. This page summarises Goel's argument, attributed to him.

sections.title: Three Jesuses, as Goel sorts them
items: Ch. 1
The Jesus of history
The search by Protestant scholars from Reimarus (18th century) to Wrede (1901). Goel says it ended in failure, citing Schweitzer.
Ch. 2
The Jesus of fiction
After the Dead Sea Scrolls and Nag Hammadi finds, a stream of reconstructions, some traced to mystery cults and myths.
Ch. 3
The Christ of faith
Bultmann's kerygma: history set aside, the proclaimed Christ kept. Goel calls it the old dogma brought back.
Ch. 4
Decline in the West
Falling church attendance and fewer priests, quoting Koenraad Elst, set against expanding missions in India.

sections.eyebrow: Chapter 1 · the silence he points to
sections.title: The historical sources, in Goel's reading and in the mainstream view

items: Philo and Justus of Tiberius never mention Jesus
He treats Josephus's references as later insertions
Seneca, Pliny the Elder, Plutarch and others are silent
Tacitus, Suetonius and Pliny the Younger refer to “Chrestus” or to Christians, not to a historical life
Josephus's shorter reference to “James, the brother of Jesus” is generally accepted as genuine
Tacitus' mention of Christ's execution under Pilate is widely taken as independent evidence
Silence about a minor Galilean preacher is unsurprising
Paul's letters, from about 20 years after the crucifixion, presuppose a historical Jesus

sections.title: What Goel asks of Hindus
items: Preface
Look at belief, not only behaviour
Hindus criticise missions and terrorism but not the creeds behind them.
Preface
Stop inventing a “real” Jesus
Praising Jesus to restrain his missionaries has not worked, he says.
Ch. 4
Dayananda, not Gandhi
Dayananda read the gospels critically; Gandhi praised Jesus while opposing conversion.
Preface
Apaddharma
Flattering an aggressor's heroes may be an emergency expedient, but should not become permanent (sanatana) dharma.
